title: Food and the gift
hook: Krishna refuses a prince's feast for a humble meal; the Gita's three kinds of food and gift
carry: sattvic food, and the gift that wants nothing back

segments.voice: Yesterday, shraddha: a person is made of faith, and faith follows nature. Today, the three threads come to the table.

Before the war, Krishna goes to Hastinapura to try for peace. Prince Duryodhana has a royal feast ready for him, hoping to win him over. Krishna turns it down. A person eats another's food, he says, when it's offered with love or when they're in need, and neither is true here. He walks to the house of Vidura, a humble, honest man, and eats there. Later, on the battlefield, the Gita sorts four ordinary things into three kinds: what you eat, how you worship, how you discipline yourself, and how you give.
screen: `A PRINCE'S FEAST, REFUSED.` → `A HUMBLE MEAL AT VIDURA'S.` → `THREE KINDS OF FOOD.`

segments.voice: Food first. Verse eight: sattvic food lengthens life and brings purity, strength, health, happiness and cheer. It's tasty, smooth, nourishing and pleasant. Verse nine: rajasic food is bitter, sour, salty, very hot, pungent, dry and burning. It brings pain, grief and sickness. Verse ten: tamasic food is stale, flavorless, spoiled, leftover, impure. Some commentators read that 'very' as reaching across the whole list, so the trouble is excess, not flavor. Then sacrifice, the offering. Sattvic: done because it ought to be done, not for a reward. Rajasic: done for the reward, or for show. Tamasic: done carelessly, without faith, without the proper words, without sharing food with others. Then austerity, tapas, discipline, in three places. Of the body: honoring teachers, cleanliness, doing no harm. Of speech, verse fifteen: words that don't upset people, that are true, kind and helpful. Of the mind: calm, gentleness, silence, self-control. Done with faith and no wish for reward, it's sattvic. Done for honor and praise, rajasic. Done to torture yourself or harm someone else, tamasic. And last, the gift. Verse twenty: a gift given simply because it should be given, to someone who can't pay you back, at the right time and place, to the right person, is sattvic. Given to get something back, or grudgingly: rajasic. Given with contempt, at the wrong time, to the wrong person: tamasic. That's why many Hindus cook fresh, simple food to offer to God before anyone eats, and why dana, the gift that wants nothing back, is honored as the highest giving.
screen: `FOOD: NOURISHING, TOO MUCH, STALE.` · `SACRIFICE: DUTY, SHOW, CARELESS.` · `AUSTERITY OF BODY, SPEECH, MIND.` · `THE GIFT THAT WANTS NOTHING BACK.` · then, large: `FOOD AND THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: Before your next meal, do what many Hindu families do: offer the plate first, in words or in your heart, and eat what comes back as prasad. If you don't pray, just notice whether this food will leave you light, buzzing, or heavy. Then hold in mind one small gift you could give someone who can't repay you, and give it this week.
Food. Gita seventeen: food, sacrifice, austerity and gift each come in three kinds, sattvic, rajasic and tamasic, and the kind shapes the one who eats, offers or gives.
Your line: sattvic food, and the gift that wants nothing back. Krishna chose the meal given with love. Day two hundred seventeen, done.

howItsDone: Many Hindus cook fresh, simple, sattvic food for an offering and offer it to God before eating (some avoid onion and garlic, especially for offerings); Gita 17.20's gift given without hope of return is cited in teaching on dana, charity.

chat.meaning: Gita 17 sorts food by its effect, and fresh, nourishing food is sattvic. Many Hindus cook simply for an offering and offer it before eating; Krishna chose Vidura's meal, given with love.

tie.story: Krishna refused Duryodhana's royal feast and ate at humble Vidura's house, because food offered with love is what he accepts.
tie.friend: Priya can tell Sam the plain plate is Nani's love made into an offering, and then everyone shares it.
tie.you: who could you give something to this week who can't pay you back?

sattvic.meaning: of the bright thread: clear, light, nourishing

rajasic.meaning: of the restless thread: driven, burning, for show

tamasic.meaning: of the heavy thread: stale, careless, dull

Vidura.meaning: a humble, honest elder at the Kuru court; Krishna ate at his house

Duryodhana.meaning: the proud Kaurava prince who led the other side

prasad.meaning: the offering handed back as a blessing

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Krishna's peace mission: he declines Duryodhana's hospitality, saying one eats another's food out of love or in need, and stays with Vidura)
Bhagavad Gita 17.11–17.19 (three kinds of sacrifice and austerity; austerity of body, speech, mind)
